'''John Lewis Rhodes''' (born July 16, 1937) is an American mathematician known for work in the theory of [[semigroup]]s, [[finite-state automata]], and algebraic approaches to [[differential equations]].<ref>[http://math.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/john-l-rhodes-0] University of California, Berkeley 2011. Retrieved 14 September 2011.</ref><ref name="mathgene">{{MathGenealogy|id=32844}}</ref>  

==Education and career==
Rhodes was born in [[Columbus, Ohio]], on July 16, 1937, and grew up in [[Wooster, Ohio]], where he founded the Wooster Rocket Society as a teenager. In the fall of 1955, Rhodes entered the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] intending to major in physics, but he soon switched to mathematics, earning his B.S. in 1960 and his Ph.D. in 1962. His Ph.D. thesis, co-written with a graduate student from Harvard, Kenneth Krohn, became known as the Prime Decomposition Theorem, or more simply the [[Krohn–Rhodes theory|Krohn–Rhodes Theorem]].<ref>Kenneth Krohn and John Rhodes,
Algebraic theory of machines. I: Prime decomposition theorem for finite semigroups and machines,
''Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.'' 116 (1965), 450-464.</ref> After a year on an [[National Science Foundation|NSF]] fellowship in [[Paris]], he became a member of the Department of Mathematics at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where he spent his entire teaching career.

In the late 1960s, Rhodes wrote ''Applications of Automata Theory and Algebra: Via the Mathematical Theory of Complexity to Biology, Physics, Psychology, Philosophy, and Games'', informally known as ''The Wild Book'',<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www-users.cs.york.ac.uk/susan/books/pages/r/JohnLRhodes.htm|title = SS > book reviews > John L. Rhodes}}</ref> which quickly became an underground classic, but remained in typescript until its revision and editing by [[Chrystopher L. Nehaniv]] in 2009.<ref>''Applications of Automata Theory and Algebra via the Mathematical Theory of Complexity to Biology, Physics, Psychology, Philosophy, and Games.'' John Rhodes. Chrystopher L. Nehaniv (Ed.). Foreword by [[Morris Hirsch|Morris W. Hirsch]]. (2009, World Scientific Books.) {{isbn|978-981-283-696-0}} (Print) {{isbn|978-981-283-697-7}} (Online)</ref> The following year Springer published his and his student Benjamin Steinberg's book, ''The q-Theory of Finite Semigroups'', both a history of the field and the fruit of eight years' development of finite semigroup theory.<ref>John Rhodes and Benjamin Steinberg (2008-12-17). ''The q-theory of finite semigroups.'' Springer Monographs in Mathematics, Springer Verlag. {{isbn|978-0-387-09780-0}} (Print) {{isbn|978-0-387-09781-7}} (Online)</ref>

In recent years Rhodes brought semigroups into [[matroid theory]]. In 2015, he published, with Pedro V. Silva, the results of his current work in another monograph with Springer, ''Boolean Representations of Simplicial Complexes and Matroids''.<ref>John Rhodes and Pedro V. Silva (2015-04). ''Boolean Representations of Simplicial Complexes and Matroids.'' Springer Verlag. {{isbn|978-3-319-15114-4}}</ref>

== Books and Monographs ==
*  John Rhodes and Benjamin Steinberg (2008), ''The q-theory of finite semigroups.'' Springer Verlag. {{isbn|978-0-387-09780-0}}.

*   John Rhodes and Pedro V. Silva (2015), ''Boolean Representations of Simplicial Complexes and Matroids.'' Springer Verlag. {{isbn|978-3-319-15114-4}}
